analysis.one_liner: Requires fully renewable electricity, all zero-emission new car sales, and regenerative farming by 2030.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in any of the three committees it was sent to; it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced large electric suppliers to sell only renewable electricity by 2030, required all new cars and trucks sold by manufacturers to be zero-emission by 2030, and required large publicly traded land and livestock companies to use regenerative farming practices. It paired these mandates with federal grants covering up to half of transition costs, doubled tax deductions for qualifying investments, and new animal welfare rules for factory farms. It was referred to three House committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and communities exposed to air pollution and climate disasters would benefit from a rapid shift to clean power, electric vehicles, and lower-emission farming. The bill's findings cite climate-driven disasters costing hundreds of billions of dollars and hitting low-income communities hardest [S3]. Electric suppliers, vehicle manufacturers, and large agribusinesses also benefit directly, receiving competitive grants covering up to 50% of compliance costs [S2] and doubled tax deductions for qualified transition spending [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People facing pollution and climate risks

how_it_helps.text: Requires retail electric suppliers selling at least 1,000 megawatt hours to reach 80% renewable electricity by 2027 and 100% by 2030, with the EPA noting that renewable energy reduces greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution from power production [S2][S3].
Requires that 80% of new motor vehicles sold by manufacturers be zero-emission starting in 2027 and 100% by 2030, cutting tailpipe pollution from cars and trucks [S2][S3].

Requires publicly traded land and livestock corporations to use regenerative agricultural practices on 50% of their land and livestock by 2025-2026, 75% by 2027-2029, and 100% by 2030, and directs USDA to write greenhouse gas reduction and animal welfare rules, including bans on routine antibiotics and physical mutilations of farm animals [S2][S3].
Cushions the transition costs with competitive grants paying up to 50% of compliance costs, priority given to suppliers and manufacturers showing significant financial need [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the grants and the doubled tax deductions, which reduce federal revenue. Electric suppliers, automakers, and large agricultural corporations bear the cost of compliance, part of which would likely be passed to customers and car buyers through higher prices [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The deadlines are far more aggressive than any existing federal requirement: 100% renewable electricity and 100% zero-emission new vehicle sales by 2030 would require a near-total rebuild of the power and auto sectors in under a decade, and critics would argue it is technically and economically infeasible on that timeline [S2][S3].

The compliance costs are partly passed through: federal grants and doubled deductions offset only part of the bill's costs, and taxpayers bear the remainder both through grant spending and forgone tax revenue, while electric rates and vehicle prices could rise [S2][S3].

The regenerative agriculture and animal welfare mandates apply only to publicly traded corporations, leaving large private and foreign-owned operators outside the rules, and the grants would route substantial public money to some of the largest agribusiness and energy companies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets more than 60% of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions — electricity, transportation, and agriculture — and its stated aim, cutting climate pollution and air pollution, serves the public broadly [S3]. But its design is aggressive to the point of raising feasibility questions: a full 100% mandate across three sectors by 2030, with transition grants capped at half of costs and the rest carried by industry and, indirectly, consumers. Even supporters would have had to acknowledge the timeline left little room for grid buildout, supply chains, or rural transition support. As introduced, it functioned as a statement of maximal ambition rather than a calibrated policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2023, referred to three House committees, and sent to two Agriculture subcommittees, but no committee ever took it up, no hearing or vote was scheduled, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Adriano Espaillat introduced the bill on January 27, 2023, with 13 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support [S1][S4].
The Speaker referred it to three committees — Agriculture, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce — meaning it needed action in any of them to move forward [S1][S5].

In February 2023, parts of it were referred to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology and the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry; no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill remained stalled in committee for the rest of the 118th Congress and died on January 3, 2025, without a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that sell fossil-fired electricity, gasoline vehicles, and conventional industrial agriculture are better off, because they avoided the 2030 mandates and the greenhouse gas, animal welfare, and non-compliance tax rules. Ordinary people gained nothing from the bill's death except the absence of its costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil power, gas-vehicle, and agribusiness interests

for.name: Rep. Adriano Espaillat
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 27, 2023, framing it as a response to climate-driven disasters and disproportionate harm to vulnerable communities [S1][S3].

for.name: 13 House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors including Reps. Velazquez, Lee of California, Nadler, and Grijalva

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup, hearing, or floor action on the bill during the two-year Congress, letting it die in committee [S5].

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Controlled committee schedules and floor time in the 118th Congress; the bill received no Republican cosponsors and no consideration [S4][S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 14 supporters were House Democrats; the bill drew no Republican cosponsors and died in committee without any vote, in a chamber controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would require retail electric suppliers to reach 100% renewable electricity by 2030, phasing out fossil generation on a fixed schedule. Its business interest runs against the public health and climate benefit the mandate targets.

Manufacturers would have to make 80% of new vehicles zero-emission by 2027 and 100% by 2030, a costly overhaul, but the bill offsets this with grants covering up to half of transition costs and doubled tax deductions. Consumers would eventually get zero-emission vehicles but could face higher near-term prices.

Publicly traded land and livestock corporations would face regenerative-practice mandates, greenhouse gas regulations, and strict animal welfare rules, but would also receive 50% cost-share grants and doubled deductions. The rules cover only publicly traded firms, leaving large private competitors untouched.

industries.industry: Renewable energy, EV, and equipment manufacturers
industries.note: The bill creates a guaranteed market — every kilowatt-hour and every new vehicle sold by 2030 — plus mandates for sourcing, recycling, and rare-earth elimination in renewable equipment. Its success depends on a dramatic scale-up of these industries.
